title: Contingent Convertible Bonds

maps.tested: Named in exactly one recall, but worth a defined-terms pass given its direct connection to the Credit Suisse AT1 write-down.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'Coco bonds.' Contingent convertibles: trigger mechanics, the equity-conversion vs. principal-write-down distinction, and the AT1-below-equity inversion controversy. Low evidence weight; low cost to cover.

vardeezReading: ORR-22: Vardeez leaves the reading untiered (the tier cell reads 0), notes that his themes Stressed market VaR (calculations) and Basel 2.5 market risk calculation land here, and says to treat it as high priority; he gives no pointer on the CoCo learning objective (ORR-22 g).

selectors.name: CoCo trigger mechanics and the 5.125% line
selectors.what: What triggers a CoCo: the Core Tier 1 to RWA ratio falling below a threshold in the indenture, or the primary regulator declaring the bank nonviable; and the classification rule that a threshold of 5.125% or higher makes the CoCo Additional Tier 1 capital, otherwise Tier 2.
selectors.theory: Conversion is set by the indenture or the regulator, never at the holder's option (that is the traditional non-financial convertible, which converts when the share price rises); the AT1 bar sits above the 4.5% Core Tier 1 minimum so the bond absorbs losses while the bank is a going concern; a Core Tier 1 trigger alone does not make a CoCo AT1.

selectors.name: Equity conversion versus principal write-down
selectors.what: The two ways a CoCo raises a bank's equity when triggered: the bond converts into shares, or its principal is written down; both increase equity, and a write-down is not equity-neutral because the liability shrinks even though no new shares are issued.
selectors.theory: CoCos are the mirror image of traditional convertibles: they raise equity in distress, not in good times; the issuer's advantage is that they stay out of the equity account until converted, giving a higher reported return on equity.

selectors.name: AT1 ranking and the inversion controversy
selectors.what: CoCo holders get little of the equity upside but bear losses not so different from equity holders when the bank fails, so CoCos should be expensive to issue; in the usual hierarchy AT1 ranks above common equity, yet in the 2023 Credit Suisse case AT1 was written down while shareholders kept some value.
selectors.theory: CoCo holders are not shielded until shareholders are wiped out; the economic cost is high, and the issuer's benefit is accounting (higher reported ROE), not a cheaper cost of capital.
